title: Math is Explaining and Sharing
contentObjective: I can construct an argument using equations, drawings, or words, and use volume to defend a recommendation.
languageObjective: I can explain my thinking with clear math vocabulary using the words argument, conjecture, and cubic units.

noticeStarters: I notice the plate holds about ___ .

vocabulary.definition: A chain of reasons — equations, drawings, or words — used to defend your thinking.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una cadena de razones — ecuaciones, dibujos o palabras — que usas para defender tu pensamiento.
vocabulary.example: I recommend two jumbo boxes because their total volume is greater.
vocabulary.cloze: A chain of reasons used to defend your thinking is an ___.

examples.text: A claim followed by the computation that supports it
examples.why: The reasons are attached to the claim.
A claim with no reasons behind it convinces nobody.

vocabulary.definition: A mathematical statement you believe is true but have not yet proven.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una afirmación matemática que crees verdadera pero que aún no has probado.
vocabulary.example: I think the two jumbo boxes hold more cereal than the three large boxes.
vocabulary.visual: “A bigger box ALWAYS holds more cereal” — believed, not yet proven.
vocabulary.cloze: A statement you believe is true but have not yet proven is a ___.

examples.text: “I think the two jumbo boxes hold more cereal.”
examples.why: It is a checkable claim that still needs an argument.
That is a definition already established, not a claim to test.

vocabulary.definition: A single example that shows a statement is not always true.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un solo ejemplo que muestra que una afirmación no siempre es verdadera.
vocabulary.example: One box with more volume but more empty air space inside.
vocabulary.visual: One jumbo box sold half full of air breaks “bigger always holds more”.
vocabulary.cloze: A single case that shows a statement is not always true is a ___.

examples.text: A larger box holding less cereal than a smaller one
examples.why: One case is enough to make the ALWAYS claim false.

examples.text: Another box that fits the claim
examples.why: Agreeing examples never disprove a statement.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of space a solid figure takes up, measured in cubic units.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La cantidad de espacio que ocupa una figura sólida, medida en unidades cúbicas.
vocabulary.example: A garden bed 4 ft long, 3 ft wide, and 2 ft deep has a volume of 24 cubic feet.
vocabulary.visual: 8 in × 3 in × 10 in = 240 cubic inches of cereal space.
vocabulary.cloze: The amount of space a solid figure takes up, in cubic units, is its ___.

examples.text: How much soil fills a 4 ft × 2 ft × 1 ft planter
examples.why: It measures the space inside, in cubic units.

examples.text: How much wrapping paper covers the box
examples.why: That is surface area — the outside, not the inside.

vocabulary.definition: A cube with edges 1 unit long — the unit used to measure volume.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un cubo cuyas aristas miden 1 unidad — la unidad que se usa para medir el volumen.
vocabulary.example: The community garden needs 48 cubic feet of soil.
vocabulary.visual: One cube, 1 unit on every edge — the block volume is counted in.
vocabulary.cloze: A cube with edges 1 unit long, used to measure volume, is a ___ ___.

examples.why: A cube 1 foot on each edge.
A square unit covers flat space; it has no depth.

launch.narrative: Yuzuki is buying her favorite breakfast cereal. She can buy three large-sized boxes or two jumbo-sized boxes for the same price. Which option should she pick — and can you convince a classmate you are right?

conceptIntro.heading: When we do math, we develop arguments to defend our thinking
conceptIntro.intro: Getting an answer is only half the work. The other half is explaining it so clearly — with conjectures, examples, and counterexamples — that someone else can decide whether your argument is convincing.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: We can defend a recommendation using equations, drawings, or words — and volume in cubic units gives the equations something exact to say.

iDo.title: Watch me argue with equations
lines: Suppose each large box is 8 inches long, 3 inches wide, and 10 inches tall. Its volume is 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 cubic inches, so three large boxes hold 240 × 3 = 720 cubic inches.
Suppose each jumbo box is 10 inches long, 4 inches wide, and 10 inches tall. Its volume is 10 × 4 × 10 = 400 cubic inches, so two jumbo boxes hold 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches.
I recommend buying two jumbo boxes because 800 cubic inches is greater than 720 cubic inches — the total volume is greater, so there is more cereal for the same price.

weDo.title: Let's argue with words together
lines: Not every good reason is an equation. Finish this argument: “I recommend buying two jumbo boxes because …”
The book offers two word-based reasons: there is less packaging with two boxes, and two boxes are easier to store than three boxes.

Now listen to the other side. One student recommends the three large boxes because the cereal will stay fresher — each box is open for less time — and because greater volume does not always mean more cereal inside.
How convincing is each argument? That judgment is math too.

youDo.title: Now you try
lines: Write one more argument for the three large boxes, and one more for the two jumbo boxes.
Then trade with a partner and say which of their arguments you find most convincing, and why.

interactiveVisual.label: The cereal box: 8 in by 3 in by 10 in.

explore.label: Which kind of argument is each statement? Sort them.

cards.text: Two jumbo boxes hold 800 cubic inches, and 800 > 720.
8 × 3 × 10 = 240, so each large box holds 240 cubic inches.
400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches for the two jumbo boxes.
There is less packaging with two boxes.
Two boxes are easier to store than three boxes.
The cereal stays fresher because each box is open for less time.
240 × 3 = 720 cubic inches for the three large boxes.
Greater volume does not always mean more cereal inside the box.

explore.instructions: Both kinds of arguments are legitimate math. After sorting, pick the one card you find MOST convincing and tell a partner why.

connect.scenario: A neighborhood group is building a community garden. To fill the beds they need soil — and to order the right amount, they need volume, measured precisely in cubic units. One design needs 48 cubic feet of soil.
connect.promptQuestion: How can the group determine the amount of soil needed, and how can they check that their answer is accurate?
connect.prompt: To find how much soil is needed, find the ___ of the garden beds. Because volume covers three dimensions, label the answer in ___ feet. Finding the volume two different ways and getting matching totals shows the solution is ___.

check.stem: The group needs to order soil to fill the garden beds. Which unit should they use to express the amount of soil?
check.explanation: Cubic feet correctly matches the beds' real-world scale. Feet only measures length (one dimension); square feet measures area (two dimensions, like a floor); cubic inches uses the right idea but too small a unit for garden-bed dimensions given in feet.

check.stem: After finding the volume of the garden beds one way, what should the group do to be confident their total of 48 cubic feet is accurate?
choices: Round the answer to the nearest ten
Decompose the figure a second, different way and check that both totals match
Multiply the total by 2 just to be safe
Ask a classmate if the number sounds right
check.explanation: Recomputing volume with an independent method and getting the same total is what actually confirms accuracy. Rounding changes the answer instead of checking it, multiplying by 2 has no mathematical reason behind it, and asking if a number 'sounds right' isn't a calculation check.

check.stem: The group decides to decompose the garden bed design into simpler shapes to find its volume. What does that method involve?
choices: Adding the areas of each face of the figure
Breaking the figure into rectangular prisms, finding each prism's volume, then adding them
Multiplying the total length by the total width only
Averaging the volumes of similar containers they've seen before
check.explanation: Decomposing means splitting the irregular figure into rectangular prisms, finding length x width x height for each piece, then summing those volumes. Adding face areas finds surface area, not volume; multiplying only length by width leaves out height; averaging unrelated containers ignores the actual dimensions.

connect.modelAnswer: I would decompose the garden beds into rectangular prisms and find each volume with length × width × height, then add them. Volume is measured in cubic units, so my answer is in cubic feet: 48 cubic feet of soil. To check accuracy I would decompose the figure a second, different way — if both ways give 48 cubic feet, the solutions match and the answer is accurate.

approaching.stem: An egg muffin is about 60 calories. A plate holds 4 egg muffins. About how many calories are on the plate?
approaching.explanation: 4 muffins at about 60 calories each is 60 × 4 = 240 calories.
choiceFeedback: That adds 60 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That divides 60 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies 60 by 10 instead of by 4.
hints: How many muffins, and how many calories in each one?
4 equal groups of 60.
Multiply 60 × 4.

approaching.stem: A large cereal box is 8 in long, 3 in wide, and 10 in tall. What is its volume?
approaching.explanation: Volume of a rectangular prism is length × width × height: 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 cubic inches.
choiceFeedback: That adds 8 + 3 + 10 instead of multiplying the dimensions.
That multiplies only 8 × 10 and leaves out the 3-inch width.
The number is right, but volume is measured in CUBIC inches — square inches measure area.
hints: Volume of a box is length × width × height.
Multiply 8 × 3 first, then use the height.

approaching.stem: Each jumbo box holds 400 cubic inches. How much do TWO jumbo boxes hold?
approaching.explanation: Two boxes of 400 cubic inches each is 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches.
choiceFeedback: That adds 400 + 2 instead of doubling.
That divides 400 by 2 instead of doubling.
That multiplies 400 by 10 instead of by 2.
hints: Two equal boxes — what operation combines them?
Double 400.

approaching.stem: Yuzuki can buy three large boxes or two jumbo boxes for the same price. Give ONE reason in words (no equations) for either choice.
approaching.modelAnswer: I recommend two jumbo boxes because there is less packaging, and two boxes are easier to store than three.
sentenceStems: A reason that is not about volume is ___ .

approaching.stem: Which unit should the garden group use when reporting how much soil fills the beds?
approaching.explanation: Volume is measured in cubic units, so soil that fills a space is measured in cubic feet.
choiceFeedback: Feet measure length — one dimension, not the space inside the bed.
Square feet measure area — the flat top of the bed, not how deep the soil goes.
Degrees measure angles or temperature, not the space soil fills.
hints: Soil fills SPACE, not a line or a flat surface.
Which unit is for volume?
Volume is measured in cubic units.

approaching.stem: Why does it help to explain your thinking to others instead of just giving the answer?
approaching.modelAnswer: When I explain my thinking, classmates can decide whether my argument is convincing, catch mistakes I missed, and connect my ideas to their own.
sentenceStems: When someone hears my reasons, they can ___ .

onLevel.stem: Three large boxes hold 240 cubic inches each. Two jumbo boxes hold 400 cubic inches each. Which is the correct volume comparison?
choices: 720 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
720 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the large option holds more
240 cubic inches vs. 400 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
480 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
onLevel.explanation: 240 × 3 = 720 and 400 × 2 = 800; since 800 > 720, the two jumbo boxes hold more in total.
choiceFeedback: The totals are right, but 800 is GREATER than 720, so the jumbo option wins the comparison.
That compares one box of each size instead of the full purchase — three larges vs. two jumbos.
480 comes from 240 × 2 — the large option has THREE boxes, not two.
hints: Find each TOTAL before comparing.
Which total is greater?

onLevel.stem: One garden bed is 4 ft long, 3 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. A second bed is 6 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. How much soil fills BOTH beds?
onLevel.explanation: First bed: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubic feet. Second bed: 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cubic feet. Together: 24 + 24 = 48 cubic feet.
choiceFeedback: 24 cubic feet is only ONE bed — the problem asks for both.
That adds all the dimensions (4+3+2+6+2+2) instead of multiplying within each bed.
That multiplies the two bed volumes (24 × ... ) too far — you ADD the volumes of the parts, you don't double the total.
hints: Find each bed's volume separately, then combine.
Add the two volumes.

onLevel.stem: The group found the volume by decomposing the garden into prisms and adding. Why would they compute it a SECOND, different way?
choices: If both ways give the same answer, the solution is accurate
Because the first way is always wrong
To get a bigger number for the soil order
Because volume changes each time you measure it
onLevel.explanation: The book models exactly this: two different decompositions both gave 48 cubic feet, so the solutions match and the answer is accurate.
choiceFeedback: The first way can be perfectly correct — the second way CONFIRMS it rather than replaces it.
Checking is about accuracy, not inflating the answer — both ways should give the SAME number.
The garden's volume is fixed — what could vary is our calculation, which is why we check it.
hints: What did the two solutions in the lesson have in common?
The solutions were the same for both ways.
Matching answers mean the calculation is accurate.

onLevel.stem: A student recommends the three large boxes because the cereal stays fresher — each box is open for less time. Is this argument convincing? Explain.
onLevel.modelAnswer: It is somewhat convincing because it uses a real reason that matters to Yuzuki, not just volume. But it would be stronger with evidence — like how long a box stays fresh once opened. An argument can be convincing without equations if the reasoning is clear.

choices: “I think the two jumbo boxes hold more cereal than the three large boxes.”
onLevel.explanation: A conjecture is a mathematical claim you believe but have not yet proven — the jumbo-box claim needs an argument to back it up.
choiceFeedback: That is a computed fact, already verified — nothing left to prove.
That is a definition, true by agreement rather than something to test.
That is a plain event from the story, not a mathematical claim to defend.
hints: A conjecture still needs proving.
Which statement says 'I think' about something checkable?
Which one would you build an argument FOR?

onLevel.stem: Use precise vocabulary to explain how you would find the soil needed for a bed 5 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. Include the answer with its unit.
onLevel.modelAnswer: I would find the volume of the rectangular prism by multiplying length × width × height: 5 × 2 × 2 = 20. Volume is measured in cubic units, so the bed needs 20 cubic feet of soil.
sentenceStems: I would find the ___ by multiplying ___ .

extending.stem: A student claims: “Greater box volume ALWAYS means more cereal inside.” Which is the best counterexample?
choices: A jumbo box with more volume that is sold half-filled with air
A large box that costs more than a jumbo box
Two jumbo boxes that are easier to store than three large boxes
A box of a different cereal brand
extending.explanation: A counterexample must break the claim itself: a bigger box holding less cereal (more air) shows greater volume does not guarantee more cereal.
choiceFeedback: Price does not test the claim — the claim links volume to AMOUNT of cereal, not cost.
Storage convenience is a different argument entirely; it says nothing about how much cereal is inside.
Changing the brand changes the product, but does not show a bigger box holding less cereal.
hints: A counterexample must make the claim FALSE in one case.
The claim connects volume to amount of cereal.
Find the case where volume is bigger but cereal is not.

extending.stem: The garden needs 48 cubic feet of soil. One decomposition used two prisms of 24 cubic feet each. Which of these is ANOTHER decomposition of the same garden volume?
extending.explanation: 4 × 4 × 2 = 32 and 4 × 2 × 2 = 16, and 32 + 16 = 48 cubic feet — the same total by a different split.
choiceFeedback: 4 × 4 × 2 = 32 twice gives 64 cubic feet, not 48.
3 × 3 × 3 = 27 and 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 give 45 cubic feet, not 48.
6 × 4 × 2 = 48 and 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 give 56 cubic feet, not 48.
hints: Compute each prism's volume, then add.
The parts must total exactly 48.

extending.stem: Another garden bed design is also being considered. What information would you need to compare the two designs, and how would you argue for the one you recommend?
extending.modelAnswer: I would need the dimensions of each design so I could compute both volumes in cubic feet. Then I would build my argument with equations — the volumes — and with words, like which design fits the space better or is easier to reach. I would state my recommendation and defend it with both kinds of evidence.

extending.stem: Write TWO arguments for the same recommendation about Yuzuki's cereal — one using equations, one using only words. Then say which you think would convince a classmate more, and why.
extending.modelAnswer: Equation argument: 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches and 240 × 3 = 720 cubic inches, and 800 > 720, so the two jumbo boxes hold more. Word argument: two boxes make less packaging waste and are easier to store. I think the equation argument convinces more people because the numbers can be checked, but the word argument matters to anyone with a small pantry.
sentenceStems: With words: ___ . The more convincing one is ___ because ___ .

practice.commonMistake: Reporting volume without cubic units — saying the garden needs '48 feet' of soil, which is a length, or '48 square feet', which is an area.

diagram.title: Which Option Holds More? (cubic inches)
diagram.caption: Three large boxes hold 240 x 3 = 720 cubic inches; two jumbo boxes hold 400 x 2 = 800. The taller bar is the evidence an equation argument would point at.

exitTicket.stem: Which statement best captures what this lesson means by 'Math is Explaining and Sharing'?
choices: We communicate our reasoning, listen to classmates' arguments, decide whether they are convincing, and check our calculations for accuracy
We keep our methods private so nobody can copy our answers
An argument only counts in math if it uses equations
Once you have an answer, checking it a second way is a waste of time
exitTicket.explanation: The summary says it directly: we communicate our reasoning, make conjectures, listen and probe classmates' arguments, communicate precisely, label units accurately, and check that our calculations are accurate.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It covers communicating, listening, precision, and checking.
Which option keeps all of those?

turnAndTalk.question: Yuzuki can buy three large boxes (240 cubic inches each) or two jumbo boxes (400 cubic inches each) for the same price. Which option gives more cereal, and how do you know?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Three large boxes hold 240 × 3 = 720 cubic inches, and two jumbo boxes hold 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches, so 800 > 720.

stems.en: Three large boxes hold ___ cubic inches, and two jumbo boxes hold ___ cubic inches.
stems.es: Tres cajas grandes contienen ___ pulgadas cúbicas, y dos cajas jumbo contienen ___ pulgadas cúbicas.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer calculates both totals (720 and 800) and compares them to recommend the jumbo boxes. A weak answer picks an option without computing and comparing both volumes.
turnAndTalk.extend: Yuzuki's friend argues 'more boxes always means more cereal.' Is she right? Use the numbers to prove your point.
extendStems: The friend is wrong because three boxes give ___ cubic inches, which is ___ than two boxes' ___ cubic inches.
This shows that number of boxes alone does not tell you ___.

turnAndTalk.question: You sorted '800 > 720' as an equation argument and 'the cereal stays fresher' as a word argument. Why are both considered legitimate math arguments, even though only one uses numbers?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The lesson treats both equation-based arguments (like 800 > 720) and word-based arguments (like less packaging) as valid ways to defend a choice.

stems.en: This is an equation argument because it uses ___.
stems.es: Este es un argumento con ecuaciones porque usa ___.

stems.en: This is a word argument because it explains ___ without numbers.
stems.es: Este es un argumento con palabras porque explica ___ sin números.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students explaining that both types of arguments can convince someone, just using different evidence (numbers vs. reasoning). A weak answer dismisses word arguments as 'not real math.'
turnAndTalk.extend: Which single card did you find MOST convincing, and what would make an argument even stronger than that one?
extendStems: The most convincing card was ___ because ___.
An even stronger argument would add ___.

turnAndTalk.question: A community garden design needs 48 cubic feet of soil. Why must the group label their answer in cubic feet instead of just 'feet'?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Volume covers three dimensions, so 48 cubic feet of soil must be labeled in cubic units, not plain feet.

stems.en: The unit must be cubic feet because volume covers ___ dimensions.
stems.es: La unidad debe ser pies cúbicos porque el volumen abarca ___ dimensiones.

stems.en: Finding the volume two different ways and getting matching totals shows the solution is ___.
stems.es: Hallar el volumen de dos maneras diferentes y obtener totales iguales muestra que la solución es ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer explains that volume measures length, width, and height together, so the unit must be cubed. A weak answer says 'because it's soil' without connecting to the three dimensions.
turnAndTalk.extend: If the garden bed were only 24 cubic feet instead of 48, would the group need more or less soil? Justify using the cubic-feet reasoning.
extendStems: With 24 cubic feet, the group would need ___ soil than before because ___.
This still uses cubic feet because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice, one problem asked about calories on a plate with 4 egg muffins at about 60 calories each. What strategy did you use to find about 240?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 4 muffins at about 60 calories each is 60 × 4 = 240 calories, using equal groups.

stems.en: I multiplied ___ by ___ to find the total calories.
stems.es: Multipliqué ___ por ___ para hallar el total de calorías.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming the multiplication strategy (4 groups of 60) rather than just stating '240.' A weak answer gives the number with no explanation.
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who added 60 + 4 instead of multiplying? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ because ___.
Their mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

questions.stem: A tram carries 10 passengers each trip. How many trips move 40 passengers?
questions.explanation: 40 passengers in groups of 10 is 40 ÷ 10 = 4 trips.
Multiplying by 10 moves each digit one place left: 2.5 becomes 25.
